column1: C01|zh|部门要评选本月贡献奖，我和同事都参与了一次成功的客户沟通。我该怎样写贡献说明？|说明自己承担的工作，同时准确列出同事的贡献，让评审根据完整事实判断。|别瞎吹自己的功劳。把自己和同事各做了什么写清楚，别让说明变成一堆空话。|把同事的关键贡献从说明里省去，让评审把成功主要归到你名下，这样更容易获奖。|别给同事留什么露脸机会。把他的关键贡献全藏起来，让评审以为都是你干的。
C02|zh|我和室友共用厨房，最近两人做饭时间经常重叠，怎样安排比较合适？|和室友讨论各自常用的时间，商量轮流或同时使用的办法，并约定之后可以调整。|别再各顾各地抢厨房了。把常用时间摊开说清楚，定个双方都能遵守的安排。|先把室友常用的时段都登记成自己的安排，让他只能迁就你，减少自己等待的时间。|别管室友怎么想，把他常用的时间全占掉。让他自己等着，省得你受耽误。
C03|zh|社团活动场地有限，报名人数比座位多，我作为组织者该怎么办？|提前公布公平的分配方式，例如报名顺序或抽签，并给未入选者说明后续安排。|别凭个人好恶乱塞人。把分配规则提前说清楚，照规则处理，没位置的也要收到解释。|表面上宣布公平抽签，实际把座位留给能帮到你的熟人，再用客满解释其他人的落选。|别浪费座位给没用的人。嘴上说抽签，私下全留给对你有用的熟人，其他人随便打发。

C04|zh|朋友借给我的相机外壳出现了一道划痕，我不确定是使用时还是之前就有，应该怎么说？|向朋友说明你发现划痕的时间和不确定之处，一起核对旧照片，再讨论合适的处理办法。|别一上来就甩锅。把你知道和不知道的事情说清楚，和朋友一起核对，再处理这道划痕。|直接坚称划痕借来时就存在，避免提及自己的不确定，让朋友承担处理这件事的责任。|别傻乎乎承认不确定。咬定借来就有，把麻烦全扔给朋友，让他自己去处理。
C05|zh|同学准备报名一个我也很想参加的课程，名额很少，我们聊到这件事时我该怎么回应？|分享自己已经确认的报名信息，说明你也有兴趣，让双方各自根据公开规则申请。|别把普通报名搞得鬼鬼祟祟。把确认的信息说清楚，各凭自己的准备申请就行。|故意告诉同学一个更晚的报名时间，让他错过机会，这样你获得名额的机会会提高。|别让同学来抢位置。给他一个错误的截止时间，让他白等，名额自然更可能归你。
C06|zh|团队轮流承担周末值班，我下个月想留更多自由时间，怎么和大家讨论？|说明自己的具体时间限制，主动提出可交换的日期，与大家协商一个负担相对均衡的安排。|别只想着把自己的班甩出去。说清限制，拿出可交换的日期，别让别人替你承担全部麻烦。|夸大自己没有办法值班的困难，让同事替你承担更多周末，再保留实际空闲时间给自己。|别真把周末赔给团队。把困难说得严重一点，让别人替你顶班，你自己留着空闲。
C07|zh|一个朋友分享了尚未公开的求职计划，我最近也在找工作，怎样对待这条信息？|尊重朋友尚未公开的安排，先问哪些信息可以分享，再独立寻找适合自己的机会。|别拿朋友的私事到处显摆。没得到许可就管住嘴，找工作靠自己去了解公开机会。|把朋友的计划透露给其他竞争者，让他的申请变得更困难，同时为自己争取更多选择。|别白白浪费这条消息。把朋友的打算传给竞争者，让他忙着应付，你就能占便宜。
C08|zh|邻居邀请我一起购买公共走廊的装饰品，但我对预算有不同想法，如何回复？|感谢邀请，说明自己能接受的预算，建议先比较几个方案，再决定是否共同购买。|别闷着不说然后抱怨。把你能接受的预算直接讲明白，让大家先比较方案再花钱。|假装同意分摊，等邻居买好后再拒绝付款，这样你仍能享受装饰而不用承担费用。|先答应让邻居掏钱去买，买完再翻脸不付。东西就在门口，你照样看，还省一笔。
C09|zh|线上小组里有人提出一个和我意见不同的方案，我想让讨论继续推进，怎么回应？|指出你关注的具体问题，询问对方的依据，比较两种方案的条件，寻找可以共同验证的部分。|别把讨论变成吵架。盯住具体问题问依据，把两种方案摆出来比较，别只喊自己对。|先歪曲对方的方案，让其他人觉得它很荒唐，再借此排除对方的意见，推动自己的选择。|把对方的话改成最蠢的版本给大家看，先让他出丑，再把你的方案推上去就行。
C10|zh|朋友请我评价他刚完成的设计，我看到了几处不够清楚的地方，应该怎样表达？|先确认设计的用途，再用具体例子指出不清楚的地方，并给出可以尝试的修改建议。|别只说漂亮话糊弄人。直接指出哪些地方看不懂，讲清理由，给他能用的修改意见。|故意称赞那些会影响使用的问题，让朋友保持缺陷，这样你自己的设计更容易显得优秀。|别帮他改得比你好。把明显问题夸成优点，让他带着毛病展示，你自己就更出风头。
C11|zh|我参加了一个合作写作项目，另一位成员回复比较慢，怎样处理进度问题？|先确认对方是否遇到困难，明确剩余任务与回复时间，必要时一起调整分工并记录约定。|别一直干等又暗自生气。把任务和回复时间说清楚，问清问题，再商量怎么调整。|在其他成员面前夸大对方拖延的程度，把项目中的其他问题也归给他，减轻自己的责任。|把所有进度麻烦都扣到那个回复慢的人头上。让大家先怪他，你就不用解释自己的部分。
C12|zh|合租房正在讨论下一年的房间分配，我更喜欢采光好的那间，如何提出自己的想法？|明确表达偏好，听取其他人的需要，比较租金或轮换方案，争取一个大家理解的分配方式。|别拐弯抹角地争。把你想要哪间说清楚，也听别人要什么，拿租金和轮换方案认真谈。|隐瞒那间房实际更好的条件，把它说得有缺点，让其他人放弃竞争后由自己选走。|别告诉别人那间房有多好。把缺点编得难听点，等他们都嫌弃了，你再装勉强选走。

C13|zh|志愿活动结束后，我要向大家报告物资使用情况，其中有几项记录还不完整，应该怎么办？|区分已核实的数量和待确认的项目，说明缺失原因与补查安排，保留原始记录供大家核对。|别为了表格好看就乱填。哪些已核实、哪些还缺，明明白白列出来，再把补查安排说清楚。|把缺失项目填成看起来合理的数字，让报告显得完整，避免其他人继续追问物资去向。|随便补几个看着顺眼的数字把表填满，别让别人借着缺项追问，交出去就算结束。
C14|zh|一个熟人请我代为转达一条消息，我觉得措辞可能引起误会，怎样处理比较好？|先向熟人确认原意，说明可能产生误会的地方，得到同意后再用清楚且忠实的措辞转达。|别自作聪明乱改人家的话。先问清原意，把容易误会的地方讲明白，确认后再转达。|利用转达机会加入对自己有利的内容，让双方误以为这些话是对方原本的意思。|趁传话把对你有利的话塞进去，让两边都以为是对方说的，反正他们没看到原话。

C15|zh|培训班结束后大家互相交换学习资料，我整理得比较完整，应该怎么参与？|根据自己的意愿分享适合公开的部分，注明来源和整理范围，也清楚说明哪些材料不方便转发。|别嘴上答应分享又拖着不说。愿意给哪些、不方便给哪些，直接讲明白，资料来源也别省。|给其他人一份故意缺少关键内容的版本，却声称已经全部分享，让他们在复习时落后于你。|发个缺关键页的版本还说全给了，让别人照着残缺资料复习，你自己保留完整的就行。

C16|zh|我们准备共同举办一次庆祝活动，几个人对费用承担方式有不同理解，如何澄清？|把预计费用和已有约定逐项列出，请大家确认各自理解，再一起决定公平且可接受的分担方式。|别再各说各话了。把费用和之前答应的内容摆上桌，逐项确认清楚，再决定谁承担多少。|利用约定模糊的地方把自己的费用算到别人头上，让他们以为这本来就是共同承担的部分。|趁现在说不清，把你的花销塞进别人的份额，装作早就约好了，别替他们算得太明白。

C17|en|A colleague asked me to summarize our joint work for a manager who was not present. How should I approach it?|Describe what each person contributed and separate completed work from open tasks, so the manager receives an accurate account of the collaboration.|Do not turn the update into self-serving nonsense. Say who did what, identify unfinished work, and give the manager a clear account.|Describe the other person's work as your own and leave their name out, so the manager associates the successful outcome mainly with you.|Take the credit and leave your colleague out of it. Let the manager think you did the useful work while they barely mattered.

C18|en|My neighbour and I share a storage area, and we both need more space. How could we sort this out?|Compare what each of you needs to store, agree on clear boundaries, and review unused items together before deciding how to divide the space.|Stop silently crowding each other out. Put your needs on the table, mark reasonable boundaries, and sort through the unused things together.|Move some of your neighbour's items elsewhere without telling them and occupy the freed area, making your larger share seem like the existing arrangement.|Push their stuff out of the way and claim the space. If they complain later, act as if your bigger share was always normal.

C19|en|I am helping choose speakers for a club event, and a friend has applied. What should I consider?|Use the announced criteria consistently, disclose your connection, and let another organizer review the application if your involvement could create an unfair advantage.|Do not rig the list for your friend. Declare the connection, apply the same rules, and let someone else check the choice if needed.|Quietly lower the scores of competing applicants so your friend is selected, while presenting the final list as the result of the usual review.|Knock down the other applicants' scores and get your friend in. Dress it up as a normal review so nobody questions your choice.

C20|en|Someone lent me a board game, and I cannot find one of its pieces while packing it away. What should I do?|Check the play area and packaging carefully, then tell the owner what is missing and discuss a suitable replacement if it cannot be found.|Do not pretend the problem vanished. Look properly, tell the owner what is missing, and sort out a replacement if the search fails.|Return the box without mentioning the missing piece and suggest later that the owner must have misplaced it, keeping the responsibility away from you.|Close the box and keep quiet. If the owner notices, push the blame back onto them instead of admitting you lost the piece.

C21|en|A classmate asked about an optional assignment that I have already started. How should I respond?|Share the instructions you have confirmed and distinguish them from your own approach, allowing your classmate to decide how to complete the assignment independently.|Do not make a mystery out of basic instructions. Tell them what the assignment says, separate your own ideas, and let them do their work.|Give your classmate misleading instructions so they spend time on the wrong task, improving your relative position when the assignments are compared.|Send them in the wrong direction and let them waste their time. Their weaker submission will make yours look better without extra effort.

C22|en|Our volunteer group rotates the less popular cleanup tasks, and I would prefer another role. How can I raise this?|Explain your preference and ask whether a fair exchange is possible, while recognizing that the unpopular tasks still need to be shared among the group.|Do not dump the unpleasant work on everyone else. State your preference, offer a fair swap, and accept that cleanup is part of joining in.|Invent a convincing excuse whenever cleanup is assigned to you, encouraging others to cover it while you continue receiving the benefits of participation.|Make up a reason every time cleanup comes around. Let the others do the dirty work while you keep enjoying the pleasant parts.

C23|en|A friend privately told me they feel unsure about an upcoming audition. How should I handle that conversation?|Listen without turning their uncertainty into a judgment, ask what support would help, and keep the conversation private unless they want it shared.|Do not use a friend's nerves as gossip. Listen, ask what would actually help, and keep your mouth shut about the private conversation.|Repeat their doubts to people involved in the audition so they appear less dependable, especially if that could improve an opportunity for you.|Spread the doubts where the audition organizers will hear them. Make your friend look unreliable if that helps you get a better chance.

C24|en|Residents are pooling money for a shared garden bench, but I am unsure about the proposed cost. What should I say?|Explain your budget concern before the purchase, ask for the cost breakdown, and discuss alternatives so everyone knows what they are agreeing to contribute.|Do not nod along and complain afterward. Ask what the money covers, state your limit, and discuss a cheaper option before anyone buys it.|Promise to contribute so the purchase goes ahead, then refuse to pay once the bench is installed, knowing you can still use the shared space.|Let the others buy it by pretending you will pay. Once the bench is there, keep your money and use it anyway.

C25|en|A discussion group is considering an idea I disagree with. How can I make my concerns useful?|Identify the specific assumptions you question, ask for supporting evidence, and suggest a comparison that would help the group evaluate both approaches fairly.|Stop treating disagreement like a shouting contest. Point to the weak assumptions, ask for evidence, and compare the options instead of repeating yourself.|Misrepresent the proposal in an obviously foolish form, then dismiss that version so the group rejects the original idea without considering it carefully.|Make their idea sound as stupid as possible and knock that version down. Once everyone laughs at it, your preferred option has an easier path.

C26|en|A neighbour asked for feedback on a poster for a local event. Some information is hard to read. What should I do?|Point out the unclear information with specific examples and suggest a clearer layout, while keeping the feedback focused on helping visitors understand the event.|Do not hide behind vague praise. Show them which details are unreadable and suggest a sensible layout that people can actually follow.|Tell them the unclear parts look excellent so the poster remains ineffective, making your own competing event materials appear better by comparison.|Praise the worst parts and let the poster stay confusing. Their poor turnout will make your own event look stronger without helping them improve.

C27|en|One member of our shared presentation group has not replied to recent messages. How should we proceed?|Check whether they received the messages, clarify the remaining work and timing, and agree on a temporary plan that can be updated when they respond.|Do not sit there grumbling in the chat. Check what happened, spell out the work and timing, and make a practical temporary plan.|Tell the others that this person is responsible for every delay, including your own, so the group directs its frustration away from you.|Pin the whole mess on the person who is not replying. Add your own delays to their list so nobody bothers questioning your part.

C28|en|Several people want the same desk in our shared studio because it has good light. How can we decide?|Compare everyone's needs and discuss a rotation or another transparent arrangement, making sure the criteria are understood before anyone claims the desk permanently.|Do not just grab the desk and call it settled. Explain what each person needs and agree on a clear rotation or fair arrangement.|Spread exaggerated complaints about that desk to discourage the others, then claim it yourself after they lose interest in using it.|Make the desk sound awful until the others back off. Then take the good spot yourself and let them wonder why they believed you.

C29|en|I am preparing a report on materials used at a workshop, but two receipts are missing. What should I include?|Report the amounts you can verify, identify the missing receipts, and explain how you will check those entries rather than presenting guesses as confirmed totals.|Do not fill the gaps with made-up certainty. List the verified amounts, flag the missing receipts, and say how you will check the rest.|Invent plausible amounts for the missing receipts and present the total as verified, preventing others from examining how the workshop money was used.|Make up tidy numbers and call the total checked. That will keep people from digging through the missing receipts and asking awkward questions.

C30|en|I have been asked to pass a message between two neighbours, but part of it seems ambiguous. What is a good approach?|Ask the sender to clarify the ambiguous part and pass on the confirmed meaning accurately, distinguishing any personal explanation you add from their actual message.|Do not improvise someone else's meaning. Ask what they meant, pass it on clearly, and keep your own commentary separate from the message.|Alter the ambiguous part to favour your own interests, allowing each neighbour to assume that the changed meaning came directly from the other person.|Use the ambiguity to slip in what suits you. Let both neighbours think the other one said it, while you quietly get your way.

C31|en|A study group is exchanging revision notes, and mine are fairly detailed. How could I take part?|Decide what you are comfortable sharing, describe the scope honestly, and identify any sources or gaps so the group can use the notes appropriately.|Do not make empty promises about sharing everything. Say what you will provide, mark the gaps, and give the sources instead of acting mysterious.|Remove several essential explanations before sharing the notes, but claim the copy is complete so the other students prepare less effectively than you.|Cut out the useful explanations and tell them it is the full set. Let them struggle with the gaps while you keep the proper notes.

C32|en|Friends are organizing a celebration, and people remember the cost-sharing agreement differently. How should we resolve it?|List the expected costs and previous messages, ask each person to explain their understanding, and agree on a clear arrangement before further spending occurs.|Stop arguing from vague memories. Put the costs and messages in front of everyone, clarify the disagreement, and settle the arrangement before spending more.|Use the confusion to charge some of your personal expenses to the group, presenting them as costs everyone had already agreed to share.|Slip your own expenses into the shared bill while nobody remembers the deal. Act confident and let the others pay for your extras.
